prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The current landscape of generalist Large Vision Models (LVMs) is dominated by architectures directly adapted from Natural Language Processing (e.g., autoregressive transformers). While successful in text, this "next-token prediction" paradigm is suboptimal for visual data. Flattening high-dimensional images or videos into one-dimensional sequences disrupts essential spatial and temporal dependencies ("spatial coherence"). Furthermore, the sequential nature of autoregressive decoding is computationally inefficient for dense visual data, as the inference time scales linearly with the sequence length. There is a need for a unified vision framework that respects the native structure of visual data while maintaining the versatility of large language models.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that a **Diffusion Transformer** framework, rather than an autoregressive one, offers a superior pathway for building a unified vision foundation model. By formulating diverse vision tasks (e.g., segmentation, depth estimation, video generation) as a conditional generative process in a continuous latent space, we can preserve spatial-temporal structure and enable parallel decoding. We further posit that integrating **in-context learning** directly into the diffusion process—where input-target pairs serve as dynamic prompts—will allow the model to generalize to arbitrary vision tasks without fine-tuning.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a unified framework ("LaVin-DiT") consisting of three strategic modules designed to handle the complexity of visual data and multi-task generalization:

1.  **Spatial-Temporal Latent Encoding (ST-VAE):**
    To manage the high dimensionality of raw pixels, we will implement a Variational Autoencoder designed specifically for spatial-temporal data. Unlike standard image VAEs, this module will utilize causal 3D convolutions. This design allows us to compress both static images and dynamic video clips into a unified, compact continuous latent space, effectively treating images as single-frame videos to maintain architectural consistency.

2.  **Joint Diffusion Transformer (J-DiT):**
    We will replace the standard backbone with a modified Diffusion Transformer optimized for task conditioning. The architecture will treat the input in two distinct streams:
    *   **Condition Stream:** Clean latent representations of "example" pairs (input-output examples defining the task).
    *   **Target Stream:** The noisy latent representation of the query input (which acts as the canvas for generation).
    
    We will implement a **Full-Sequence Joint Attention** mechanism. This module will concatenate the condition and target sequences, allowing the model to bidirectionally attend to the task examples while denoising the target. This ensures the generation is strictly aligned with the task defined by the context examples.

3.  **3D Spatial-Temporal Awareness:**
    To strictly avoid the pitfalls of 1D sequence flattening, we will discard standard 1D positional embeddings. Instead, we will employ **3D Rotary Position Encodings (3D RoPE)**. This allows the model to explicitly understand the spatial (x, y) and temporal (t) coordinates of every patch, preserving the geometric and dynamic structure of the data throughout the network.

4.  **In-Context Training Strategy:**
    The model will be trained using a "visual prompting" strategy. We will sample input-target pairs from various datasets to serve as the context. The model's objective is to reconstruct the target output for a specific query using flow matching, guided solely by the relationships inferred from the context pairs.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Unified Generalist Architecture:** A single model capable of performing over a score of image and video tasks (from segmentation to frame prediction) using a standardized input format.
*   **Efficiency via Parallelism:** By leveraging diffusion modeling, we expect to achieve parallel decoding of visual tokens, offering significantly lower inference latency compared to autoregressive counterparts.
*   **Structural Preservation:** The use of continuous latent spaces and 3D positional encodings is expected to yield higher fidelity in tasks requiring precise spatial and temporal coherence.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive experimental framework to evaluate the proposed Large Vision Diffusion Transformer (LaVin-DiT).

*   **Training Data:**
    *   We constructed a large-scale multi-task dataset comprising approximately 3.2 million unique images and 0.6 million unique videos.
    *   The dataset covered over 20 tasks, including:
        *   **Image-based:** Object detection, instance segmentation, panoptic segmentation, pose estimation, edge extraction, depth estimation, surface normal estimation, inpainting, colorization, image restoration (deraining, de-glass blur, de-motion blur), depth-to-image, and normal-to-image generation.
        *   **Video-based:** Frame prediction, video depth estimation, video surface normal estimation, video optical flow estimation, video instance segmentation, depth-to-video, and normal-to-video generation.
    *   Pseudo-labels for depth and surface normal estimation were generated on ImageNet-1K using Depth-anything V2 and Stable-Normal (turbo), respectively.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Architecture:** The default model used for reporting main results contained 3.4B parameters. We also trained 0.1B and 1.0B variants for scalability analysis.
    *   **Hardware:** All experiments were conducted on 64 $\times$ NVIDIA A100-80G GPUs.
    *   **Optimization:** We utilized DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 optimization and gradient checkpointing. The optimizer was AdamW with betas set to 0.9 and 0.95, and weight decay of 0.01.
    *   **Training Schedule:** Training occurred in two stages:
        *   *Stage 1:* Resolution $256 \times 256$, 100,000 steps, global batch size 640, learning rate 0.0001. No warmup was used.
        *   *Stage 2:* Upscaled resolution to $512 \times 512$, trained for an additional 20,000 steps, learning rate adjusted to 0.00005.
    *   **Inference:** We used 20 timesteps ($N = 20$) by default. The inference process utilized task-specific context sets (input-target pairs) and test data as queries.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Foreground Segmentation & Single Object Detection:** Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) (Higher is better).
    *   **Colorization:** Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) (Lower is better).
    *   **Depth Estimation:** Absolute Relative difference (AbsRel) (Lower is better) and Threshold Accuracy ($\delta_1$) (Higher is better).
    *   **Surface Normal Estimation:** Mean Angular Error (MAE) (Lower is better) and Angle Accuracy within threshold $< 11.25^{\circ}$ (Higher is better).
    *   **Inpainting:** Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) (Lower is better).
    *   **Latency:** Seconds per example.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   MAE
    *   MAE-VQGAN
    *   LVM (Large Vision Model) - specifically the 7B parameter version was used for Table 2 comparisons.
    *   DPT
    *   StableNormal
    *   Marigold

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Comparison on Foreground Segmentation, Single Object Detection, and Colorization**
*Note: Foreground segmentation and single object detection were unseen tasks during training.*

| Method | Seg Split 1 (mIoU) | Seg Split 2 (mIoU) | Seg Split 3 (mIoU) | Seg Split 4 (mIoU) | Det Split 1 (mIoU) | Det Split 2 (mIoU) | Det Split 3 (mIoU) | Det Split 4 (mIoU) | Colorization MSE | Colorization LPIPS |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MAE | 17.42 | 25.70 | 18.64 | 16.53 | 5.49 | 4.98 | 5.24 | 5.84 | 0.43 | 0.55 |
| MAE-VQGAN | 27.83 | 30.44 | 26.15 | 24.25 | 24.19 | 25.20 | 25.36 | 25.23 | 0.67 | 0.40 |
| LVM | 48.94 | 51.29 | 47.66 | 50.82 | 48.25 | 49.60 | 50.08 | 48.92 | 0.51 | 0.46 |
| **LaVin-DiT** | **67.87** | **75.80** | **66.98** | **66.90** | **67.85** | **69.32** | **68.76** | **68.88** | **0.24** | **0.26** |

**Table 2: Comparison on NYU-v2 Depth Estimation, Surface Normal Estimation, and ImageNet Inpainting**
*Note: The LVM baseline denoted here used the official 7B model.*

| Method | Depth AbsRel ($\downarrow$) | Depth $\delta_1$ ($\uparrow$) | Normal MAE ($\downarrow$) | Normal $< 11.25^{\circ}$ ($\uparrow$) | Inpainting FID ($\downarrow$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DPT | 9.8 | 90.3 | - | - | - |
| StableNormal | - | - | 19.707 | 53.042 | - |
| Marigold | 6.0 | 95.9 | 20.864 | 50.457 | - |
| LVM (7B) | 30.2 | 52.3 | 23.433 | 44.836 | 4.05 |
| **LaVin-DiT** | **6.2** | **96.1** | **15.901** | **58.382** | **1.65** |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Model Architecture and Concept Analysis**
*   We observed that autoregressive modeling (processing tokens sequentially) disrupted spatial dependencies and was computationally intensive for high-dimensional visual data.
*   In contrast, we found that diffusion modeling (denoising all tokens in parallel) preserved essential spatial structures and improved computational efficiency.
*   The architecture utilized a spatial-temporal variational autoencoder (ST-VAE) to compress pixel space into latent space, and a Joint Diffusion Transformer (J-DiT) to denoise the target latent representation guided by task context.

**Visual and Task Performance Observations**
*   **General Performance:** The model consistently followed task contexts to generate precise predictions across diverse image-based tasks (segmentation, pose, depth, normals) and video-based tasks (frame prediction, video depth).
*   **Temporal Consistency:** Given sequential frames with task contexts, the model successfully generated predictions for subsequent frames (e.g., 12 frames), effectively maintaining temporal consistency and scene dynamics.
*   **Unseen Tasks:** We observed significant margins over the LVM baseline on unseen tasks. For Single Object Detection (Split 4), our model achieved a mIoU of 68.88%, surpassing LVM by 19.96%.
*   **Inpainting:** We achieved an FID of 1.65 on 2,500 ImageNet-1K validation images, compared to 4.05 for LVM.

**Scalability Analysis**
*   **Training Convergence:** We compared models with 0.1B, 1.0B, and 3.4B parameters. We observed that larger models consistently achieved lower loss values. The 3.4B model converged more rapidly than smaller variants.
*   **Metric Scaling (Colorization):** Performance improved with model size.
    *   0.1B model: MSE 0.609
    *   1.0B model: MSE 0.311
    *   3.4B model: MSE 0.273
*   **Metric Scaling (Depth Estimation):**
    *   0.1B model: AbsRel 7.6
    *   1.0B model: AbsRel 6.5
    *   3.4B model: AbsRel 6.2

**Inference Latency Analysis**
*   We compared inference latency between LaVin-DiT (7B) and LVM (7B) across resolutions using 8 input-target pairs on an A100-80G GPU.
*   **Resolution 256:** LaVin-DiT required 4.67 seconds per example; LVM required 8.1 seconds.
*   **Resolution 384:** LaVin-DiT required 10.2 seconds; LVM required 19.3 seconds.
*   **Resolution 512:** LaVin-DiT required 20.1 seconds; LVM required 47.2 seconds.
*   We observed that the efficiency gap widened at higher resolutions, attributed to the parallel nature of diffusion versus the sequential nature of autoregressive models.

**Effect of Task Context Length**
*   We analyzed the impact of increasing the number of input-target pairs (from 1 to 8) on ten downstream tasks.
*   **Observation:** Increasing task context length consistently improved performance across all tested metrics.
    *   Colorization (MSE) decreased.
    *   Inpainting (LPIPS) decreased.
    *   Depth Estimation (RMSE) decreased.
    *   Surface Normal Estimation (Mean Error) decreased.
    *   Depth2Image Generation (FID) decreased.
    *   Normal2Image Generation (FID) decreased.
    *   Single Object Detection (mIoU) increased.
    *   Foreground Segmentation (mIoU) increased.
    *   Deraining (PSNR) increased.
    *   De-motion Blur (PSNR) increased.

The model then predicts each token sequentially from left to right and top to bottom, which is computationally intensive for high-dimensional visual data. Besides, tokens marked in red and blue illustrate disrupted spatial dependencies, highlighting the limitations of preserving spatial coherence. (b) In contrast, diffusion modeling denoises all tokens in parallel across N timesteps, significantly improving computational efficiency and preserving essential spatial structures crucial for high-performance vision tasks.

A set of frames in the red box indicates the model’s predictions. Best viewed in color.
--------------------------------------------------

  - Caption: Figure 5. Performance for LaVin-DiT of varying sizes. Comparison of LaVinDiT with different parameters on colorization (MSE) and depth estimation (AbsRel). Lower values indicate better performance.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 5:
  - Filename: figure_6.png
  - Caption: Figure 6. Inference latency comparison. LaVin-DiT consistently achieves lower latency than LVM [4] across different resolutions, as tested on an A100-80G GPU with 8 input-target pairs.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 6:
  - Filename: figure_7.png
  - Caption: Figure 7. Effect of task context length. Longer task context can consistently improve the performance of downstream tasks.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 7:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Overview of Large Vision Diffusion Model (LaVin-DiT). As shown in panel (a), the model initially compresses input visual data from the pixel space into a latent space, where multiple input-target pairs serve as the task context. A target is perturbed with Gaussian noise through a diffusion process. Guided by the task context and query, the Joint Diffusion Transformer (J-DiT) iteratively denoises this noisy target over N timesteps to recover a clean latent representation. The prediction is then generated via the ST-VAE decoder. Panels (b) and (c) provide architectural details of the ST-VAE and J-DiT, respectively. “Down.” and “Up.” indicate the downsampling and upsampling, respectively. Concatenation is represented by ⊙.
--------------------------------------------------

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

```latex
  \end{subfigure}

  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current efforts to develop Large Vision Models (LVMs) capable of generalizing across multiple tasks largely rely on adapting architectures from Natural Language Processing (e.g., GPT). Specifically, these approaches treat visual data as 1D sequences of tokens and utilize autoregressive modeling. This paradigm presents two critical limitations:
1.  **Computational Inefficiency:** Autoregressive prediction requires sequential token-by-token processing, which is prohibitively expensive for high-dimensional visual data.
2.  **Disrupted Spatial Coherence:** Flatenning 2D images or 3D videos into 1D sequences disrupts local spatial dependencies, which are fundamental to computer vision performance.

There is currently no unified framework that efficiently handles the high dimensionality of vision data while preserving spatial-temporal structure in a generalist, multi-task setting.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **LaVin-DiT**, a unified Large Vision Diffusion Transformer. We hypothesize that by replacing autoregressive sequential modeling with a **Joint Diffusion Transformer (J-DiT)**, we can treat visual generation as a parallel denoising process. This will improve computational efficiency and preserve spatial structure.

Furthermore, to enable generalist capabilities without task-specific fine-tuning, we will implement **In-Context Learning** within the diffusion framework. By providing the model with input-target pairs as a context, the model will learn to align its output distribution to the target task (e.g., depth estimation, segmentation) dynamically.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a conditional generative framework designed to model the conditional distribution $p(\pmb{y} | \pmb{x}, \pmb{s})$, where $\pmb{x}$ is the query (image/video), $\pmb{y}$ is the target output, and $\pmb{s}$ is a set of input-target pairs acting as the task definition.

### 1. Spatial-Temporal Variational Autoencoder (ST-VAE)
To mitigate the computational demand of raw pixel space, we will construct a Spatial-Temporal VAE to compress data into a compact latent space.
*   **Architecture:** The ST-VAE will utilize causal 3D convolutions and deconvolutions arranged in symmetric encoder-decoder stages.
*   **Compression Strategy:** We will implement alternating downsampling/upsampling. The first two stages will operate on both spatial and temporal dimensions, while the final stage will operate only on the spatial dimension.
*   **Temporal Independence:** To support both image and video inputs seamlessly, the first frame of any video input will be compressed only spatially. Subsequent frames will be compressed along both spatial and temporal dimensions.
*   **Regularization:** We will apply a Kullback-Leibler (KL) constraint to regularize the latent space towards a Gaussian distribution.

### 2. Joint Diffusion Transformer (J-DiT)
The core generative module will be a Transformer tailored for flow matching.

**Input Processing:**
We distinguish between two latent representations:
1.  **Condition Latent ($z_c$):** The clean representation of the context set $\pmb{s}$ and input $\pmb{x}$.
2.  **Target Latent ($z_t$):** The representation of $\pmb{y}$ perturbed by Gaussian noise.

To address distinct value ranges between clean and noisy latents, we will employ **separate patch embedding layers** (patch size $2\times2$) for the condition and target latents.

**Adaptive Normalization (AdaRN):**
We will implement condition- and target-specific Adaptive RMS Normalization. This module will accept distinct timestep embeddings to modulate the representation space of the condition and target independently.

**Full-Sequence Joint Attention:**
Instead of cross-attention, we will implement a full-sequence joint attention mechanism.
1.  Condition and target sequences will be linearly projected and concatenated.
2.  A bidirectional attention module will process the combined sequence, allowing mutual interaction in a shared space.
3.  **Optimization:** We will utilize **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)** to reduce parameters while maintaining expressiveness.
4.  **Stabilization:** We will insert **QK-Norm** (normalization before query-key dot products) and **Sandwich Normalization** (after attention and FFN layers) to control entropy growth and activation magnitudes during training.

**3D Rotary Position Encoding (3D RoPE):**
To avoid the limitations of 1D embeddings, we will implement 3D Rotary Position Encoding. This allows us to represent the precise spatial-temporal coordinates of patches within the continuous sequence of image-annotation pairs or video clips.

### 3. Training Formulation: Conditional Flow Matching
We will train J-DiT using Flow Matching to regress a velocity field $v$ that transforms a noise distribution into the data distribution.

We define the forward linear interpolation process as:
$$ z_t = t z_0 + (1 - t) z_1 $$
where:
*   $t \in [0, 1]$ is the timestep.
*   $z_0$ is the clean data representation.
*   $z_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ is the noise.

This process induces a flow defined by the Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE):
$$ \mathrm{d}z_t = v(z_t, t) \mathrm{d}t $$

We will parameterize the J-DiT with parameters $\pmb{\theta}$ to predict the velocity field. The training objective, **Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) loss**, is defined as:
$$ \ell_{\mathrm{CFM}} = \int_0^1 \mathbb{E} [ | v_{\pmb{\theta}}(z_t, t) - (z_0 - z_1) |_2^2 ] \mathrm{d}t $$

### 4. Inference Procedure
For generation, we will integrate the learned velocity field backward from $t=1$ to $t=0$. Using the Euler method with $N$ steps and step size $\Delta t = -1/N$, the update rule at step $k$ will be:

$$ \begin{array}{rl} & t^{(k+1/N)} = t^{(k)} + \Delta t, \\ & z^{(k+1/N)} = z^{(k)} + v_{\pmb{\theta}}(z^{(k)}, t^{(k)}) \Delta t, \end{array} $$

where $z^{(0)}$ is sampled from noise. The final $z^{(1)}$ is passed to the ST-VAE decoder to recover the pixel-space prediction.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Unified Generative Framework:** We aim to establish a single model capable of performing over 20 diverse vision tasks (image and video) solely through in-context learning, removing the need for task-specific heads.
2.  **Architectural Novelty:** The proposal of J-DiT with full-sequence joint attention and 3D RoPE is expected to solve the spatial coherence issues inherent in autoregressive LVMs.
3.  **Scalability and Efficiency:** By leveraging parallel decoding via diffusion, we anticipate significantly lower inference latency compared to autoregressive baselines, particularly at high resolutions.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
